questions.q: Wild yeasts of several genera often begin a spontaneous fermentation. Which species usually takes over and finishes it?
questions.exp: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the species the Court names for wine fermentation, tolerates rising alcohol far better than the wild yeasts of other genera that start a ferment from the grape skins and the cellar, so it takes over once the alcohol passes a few per cent and finishes the job. It is the same species that raises bread and ferments ale.

questions.q: Besides oak, which of these woods is coopered into barrels by some cellars, chiefly for white wine?
questions.exp: Acacia barrels are used in parts of Burgundy, the Loire and Friuli for whites, adding a floral, honeyed note with little tannin. The Court also names cherry and chestnut among the other woods used for barrels; pine, eucalyptus and birch are not coopered for wine.

questions.q: Of the barrel sizes the Court lists, which vessel is the largest, at a thousand litres and more?
questions.exp: The Court's ladder is barrique 225 litres, puncheon 300, demi-muid 600 and foudre, or botti in Piemonte, 1,000 litres and more. The bigger the vessel the less wood touches each litre, so a large old foudre marks a wine far less than a new barrique, the cask of Rioja and Bordeaux.

questions.q: Which sulphur compound in a finished wine actively guards it against oxidation and spoilage microbes?
questions.exp: Free sulphur dioxide, whose molecular form is the most active, is what protects a wine against oxygen and spoilage microbes; once it combines with acetaldehyde, sugars and other compounds it is bound and protects no longer. Total sulphur dioxide is the free and the bound together, and the Court asks the difference between them.

questions.q: Which of these whites is most likely to show the butter and cream notes the Court's grid files under malolactic fermentation?
questions.exp: Oaked Chardonnay from California commonly goes through full malolactic conversion, which softens its acidity and brings the buttery note of diacetyl. Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc and Albariño are usually kept from it to hold their crisp acidity and primary fruit, so the grid's malolactic line should read No for them.

questions.q: Winemaking that shuts air out with inert gas, cool steel tanks and sealed vessels, to keep primary fruit fresh, is described by what term?
questions.exp: Reductive winemaking keeps oxygen away to hold primary fruit and aroma, as in a crisp Sauvignon Blanc; oxidative winemaking lets air in on purpose through barrels, racking and ullage, building nutty, developed flavours, with Oloroso and tawny Port at the far end. The Court asks the difference between the two.

questions.q: Which two sugars make up nearly all of the sugar in ripe grapes?
questions.exp: Ripe grape juice holds glucose and fructose in roughly equal amounts, the sugars yeast ferments into alcohol; sucrose, the cane or beet sugar of chaptalisation, is split into the same two before yeast can use it. Yeast takes glucose a little faster, so the sugar left in a sweet wine leans towards fructose, the sweeter of the two.
